racing season around the metropoli-

day, has clearly shown that the pub

tracks in the last three months has
demonstrated this. The crowds have
been far above the average of those
of recent years, and all previous rec

The only jarring note of the season
just closed has been found in the SELL
ing races. These events have been
the means Of creating a war among a
certain class of horsemen who make
practice of claiming and bidding up
the horses of their competitors and
thereby placing money in their own
pockets. But the stewards of the
Jockey Club have the matter in hand
and in all probability they will amend
the rules governing these races in a
way to give general satisfaction and
at the same time minimize the un-
sportsmanlike phase of this feature of
racing.


The racing itself has been excep-
tionally good and many new stars
have been developed in the various
divisions. Horses are once more
plentiful and the field of competi-
tion has improved with each meet

are particularly rich in high-class
material In the former. many prom
ising Juveniles have been shown. and
there are a lot more yet to be seen.
as numerous owners are opposed to
starting their youngsters too early in
the season. These will be seen at
the Saratoga meeting. where there are
a plentiful supply of rich events for
s-year-olds.


Among the 3-year-olds are nu-
merous high-clsss horses which have
been racing around New York the
last three months and their perform
ances indicate that the present day
thoroughbred Is every bit as fast as
the racers of former years. Such
horses as Friar Rock. Star Hawk,
Spud, Churchill. Celandria and others
will compare favorably with the best
which raced in former years in this
division. The same condition exists
In the older classes. where we have
the old champion Romer. Short Grass
Sand Marsh, Trial by Jury. Harry
Shaw. and others which have proved
their stamina and gameness over a
distance of ground.

A wonderful spectacle of war was visible
today from a high point near the junction
OF the French and British armies.


To the north lay a dark patch which
was the ruins of Gulllemont. frlnged by the
wave-lllSe earthly lines of the old second
line of German trenches facing Trones

For six weeks the British had burrowed
against the Germans over this shell-rup-
turcd, bullet-ridded field. Yesterday was
the day of the successful British effort TO
break through the German bulwark.


British artillery had not destroyed all the
dcep dugouts, but their curtain of intensi-
fed shell fire kept the machine gunners
down and out of these dugouts. and after
half an hours work British infantry turned
some coo prisoners

perhaps treble the distance from home plate

oil that Is another patch OF ruins that was
once the village of Gnchy, where fghting



and forth between the barr cades and cell
lars and any old kind of cover the men
could throw up out of the debris.


The British seem firmly established on
the sunsen road. All night they were dig
Ring themselves holes there. This was
their objective no less than Is second base
TO runner on q two-base hit. II they
tried to 20 farther because the going was
good they might be put out. That happened
yesterday at some points of attack. as 1t
sometimes does. thanks to overeagerness'
Disorder results, the men get out from under
the protection of their own gunflre and are
cut up. -


BAYONET FIGHTING


At tho southern end of the sunken road
Is a finger pont--a green wedge of woods.
and below this is the Falfanont farm,
where the British attack stopped yesterday.
Here the Prussian guard left the trenches
in a charge to meet the British charge half
way.


Thus they came to the bayonet The
big guns could send no shells nor could
the machine guns send any bullets for fear
of hitting their own men. All the
engineery of war with It's missiles that
kill men at long range formed a ring
around these comba tants, who fought prac-
ticaly to extinction with the cold steel.


Today. around Falfemont farm. the pic
ture was intimate yet incomprehensible TO
observers in its ebb and How of attack
The contrast of British and Prussan meth
ods were set out as'in panorama A-..


The British charge moved up with each
unit seeming to act for itself, yet keeping
the formation and then came the German
counter-attack in regular wave, followed
by another dipping with the undulating
ground. Figures in the first wave began
TO drop as the British machine guns began
to rattle, bus the second wave still came
on in a way that made British officer
with characteristic sportsmanship exclaim:
Magnificent! Topping! -


A CONFUSED PICTURE.


The second wave melted on the ground
where the first wave had disappeared, but
the results were confused. The observer
could only tell that charges were met by
counter-charges while machine guns, in
hidden places, waited for their game with
their murderous blasts 1t could not al
ways be told whether figures leaving their
trenches were men retreating or prisoners
under escort. Fast-running figures from
either side ta-the rear were either messen-
gers sending back word OF the situation
TO commanders when all other signals failed
TO work. or they were running to get more
bombs, whose puffs OF smoke were visible
here and there.


Would these gallant fellows get through
without being hit? was the question as
they were lost in the midst of shell smoke.


Farther south, the blue Of the French
mingled with the .khakl OF the British and
the men appeared and disappeared In the
earth like ants. Back of the lines French
and British guns and transp' rts mingled
and British wounded and French wounded
came along the same paths with German
prisoners. sometimes British litter-bearers
taking Frenchmen and French sometimes
taking Britons. Groups of British soldiers
cheered the French after their success OF
yesterday


General Foch's steel-throated orators
were very busy down there In the green
lowlands of the winding Somme, where
Bhrapnel smoke lay feathery white against
the foliage fresh from the nights rain, and
across the Somme, as far as the eye could
see, ran this canopy Of flashes from guns
that seemed to answer with regular hring
20 the touch OF some master hand, Nearer
and nearer to PerOnne that swath or fire
moves with every battle.


The Germans didn't know how many
guns Father Joffre had up his sleeve" said

Turning first to the map, it is now plain
what has happened. When the recent at
tack began the eastern front followed the
Dwina River from the outskirts of the city
Of Riga, speaking very roughly here, to the
city of Dvinsk approximately an east and
west front; then it turned sharply south
and ran pretty nearly straight through
Pinsk, which the Germans held, through
the Pripet marshes, along the Styr River,
east of Lutsk and Dubno, which were Aus
trian, along the Sereth River just west of
Tarnopol, which was Russian, to the Dnies-
ter River, and thence to the Pruth River
lust west of the Russian frontier.


Now, from the Gulf Of Riga to the Pripet
marshes and TO the southern border of this
swamp the line still stands, but a little
south Of the marshes begins very wide,
deep curve which the Russians have driven
westward.


This curve amounts to a semi-circle,
drawn about Dubno, with a radius of per
haps thirty-fve miles, which represents
the extreme penetration of the Russian
into the Austrian front. Going south
again there is a second semi-circle of per
haps twenty-five miles radius, from the
point where the Dniester reaches the Rus
sian frontier. As the northern curve ex-
tends toward Kovel and vladimir Wolyn-
ski, the southern passes southwest of Ger
nowitz and is approaching Kolomea.


These two semi-circles, to use the mill
tary parlance, are the wedges which the
Russians have driven into the Austrian
lines, after having successfully broken the
trench front which was in their immediate
front. The war in these sectors has thus
become a war Of movement as contrasted
with the trench operation. To use famil-
lar figure, these two circles represent
breaks in the dixie the Central Powers had
erected against the Slavonic flood; through
these breaks the Russian waters are now
sweeping and extending not only west
ward but tending to swirl round the ends
Of the dixie and expand north and south in
the fashion of fan.

Columbian agree that the German subsea
commander not only ignored the American
nag when it was run up at the Coumbian's
masthead, but that he also refused even to
hear Captain Curtis's plea for the protec-

Captain Curtis, at dinner when he heard

blockade only became really effective

tin. through Sweden. Denmark and
Norway. Importers here are convinced

ELGIN, Ariz., with District Signal
Corps wagon train, overland from Bis
bee to Nogales. October Although
cautioned to fill their canteens before
they left Fort Huachuca yesterday,
number of members of the District
Signal Corps Company did not heed the
instructions. Today they knew, many
of them for the first time. what it
means to have a thirst that only a
drink of water will quench.


After a long march over rough and
dusty roads, intensified by the horses
hoofs, which kept a cloud over the
command at all times, the boys began
to feel the need of water. Many had
not even taken the trouble to fill their
canteens before they left the last camp
ing ground. while others, wasted it on
the way. They were warmed by their
comrades who had seen border service
before that they would need it before
they had gone far, and they did. There
was nothing for them to do but wait.


Many small streams were crossed on
the way, but only the animals were al
lowed to drink there The strict sanitary
precautions taken to protect the health
of the soldiers forbid their drinking any
water from open streams, except where
the water had been filtered and other
wise Sterilized.


Have Learned Lesson Well.


These streams had not received the Of
fetal O. X. of the medical department,
so the men had to go without, except for
small amounts that they could persuade
their comrades with filled canteens to
give them. 1t was a lesson that they will
not forget


Both men and animals showed the eff
fects of the long, hard march over the
bad roads between Fort Huachuca and
this place. The wagon train which fol-
lowed the command found it particu-
larly difficult travelling, but finally reached
the camp, only a short time behind the
main body.


Early tomorrow morning the command
will begin the last leg OF it's journey, be-
ing under orders to report at old Fort
Crittenden. There Capt Oliver c. Terry,
commanding the organization, will re-
ceive his orders telling what part the
District organization will play in the big
maneuvers. The men are well seasoned
and are expected TO give good account
of themselves in any problem which will
be given them.

From the National Geographic Magazine.


The walruses or "sea horses" of the
old navigators are the strangest and
most grotesque of all sea mammals.
Their large, rugged heads, armed with
two long ivory tusks, and their huge
swollen bodies, covered with hairless.
wrinkled and warty skin, give them
formidable appearance unlike that Of
any other mammal. They are much
larger than most seals, the old males
weighing from 1000 to 1000 pounds
and the females about two-thirds as
much.


walruses have a strongly developed
maternal instinct and show great devo-
tion and disregard OF their own safety
in defending the young. The Eskimos
at Cape Vancouver, Bering sea, hunt
them in frail skin-covered kyaks. using
ivory-or bone-pointed spears and
sealskin floats Several hunters told
me of exciting and dangerous encoun-
ters they had experienced with mother
walruses. If the young are attacked.
or even approached, the mother does
not hesitate to charge furiously. The
hunters confess that on such occasions
there is no option but to paddle for
ones life. Occasionally an old walruS
is unusually vindictive and, after fore
ing a hunter to take refuge on the ice,
will remain patrolling the vicinity for
long time, roaring and menacing the
object of her anger.

Two postoffice safe robberies within the

perpetrators.


The safes opened were both on line of
the Philadelphia and Reading Railway.
one at Red Hill. Montgomery County,
the other at Woodbourne, near Lang
horne, Bucks County.


Nitroglycerin was used in each case
Nearly $500 in booty was obtained by the
robbers, who forced their way into the
postoffices by breaking open the front
door. From the Red Hill postofice
stamps worth $500 and $3.50 in cash was
taken. At Woodbourne the robbers got
S23S worth of stamps and $50 in cash.


The police and Government officials,
who are also investigating, are convinced
that the same men were responsible for
both jobs. Stolen tools were used in each
case to break into the pOstOffices.


The robbers spent the night in the Maple
Point Public School. where they forced
an entrance after completing the Wood
bourne job. A pile OF cigarette stumps
pointed to their presence there, but they
stole nothing.


Examination of the safes after the rob-
berries convinces the police that the rob-
berries were the work of expert safe
crackers.

text:
Ten more tiny wayfarers came back
from the grim borders of plagueland
yesterday afternoon in the Willard
Parker Hospital, at the foot of East
Sixteenth Street, where one thousand
infantile paralysis patients are con-
fined.


Most Of them did not return from
the far country as they had gone into
it. Their twisted legs were in plaster
casts or on splnts, and their baby
faces sometimes distorted with pain,
when they were carried into the room
where their parents sat eagerly await
ing them. Some will not recover for
years, and some will never walk again.
Not one of them is four years old.


Tommy Is a Hero.


Tommy was hero of the day. He is
Thomas Keegan, three years old if you
please, and the mark on his card vas
80. X" He was the only one who came
out entirely cured. Parents crowded
about him enviously and handled his
sturdy limbs with jealous fingers.
Tommy didn't like attention and, being
Irish, struck out with furious fists.
The other fathers and mothers turned
to their own children with tears in
their eyes.


The information room from which
the patients were sent out was crowd
ed. Parents whose babies were to be
given 70 them, parents with babies i'll
or dying, were there. Outside was the
long, tragic row of mothers who come
four times a day to nurse their chill
dren. They peered fesrfully and visit
fully at the little ones who were car
ried out.


Parents Brought Dolls.


When a child is to be released from
hospital, which happens eight weeks
after he enters it, the parents are in
formed by telegraph. When they come
they bring the clothes that he is 10
wear away. All these little dresses
yesterday were new, and most of them
were gaily adorned with pink and blue
ribbons, probably prettier clothes than
the child had ever had. Most Of the
mothers brought along the youngsters
favorite doll TO welcome the patient
back.


The first child carried out was Rosie
Sebastian, who was cured except for
slight facial paralysis. Seeing how well
she looked, a cheer went up from the
line of parents. Rosie's mother took
her baby proudly, while Rosie's father
made a clumsy effort to tie on her
brand new bonnet, and Rosie's aunt
came forward with a doll.


Kisses Attendants.


Two-year-old Elizabeth Calls, who
came next, was able TO walk. Her case
had been considered hopeless. The
sacrament had been administered, and
her mother said that for a month she
had prayed nightly that the child
might die. Her little sister WAS a VIC
tim of the plague, and her nnrsemald
is still in hospital with il. Elizabeth
insisted upon kissing all the attendants
goodby.


Let me get out of this" said man
who had come TO have the death certif-
, cate of his baby made out.
The next child had both legs in
splints. Her mother did not notice un-
til an attendant called them TO her at
tention. Then she sat on bench,
buried her face in her arms and refused
to be comforted.


81 guess I'm lucky the other six
haven't got it, too" she said after
time.


Many Crippled.


Another child wore the braces that
it can never be without. baby thirteen
months old had its legs in splints,
and another was paralyzed in its facial
muscles and its left leg.


Many parents who did not speak Eng
lish could not understand why their
children were held.


Fathers and mothers were allowed TO
see their children once. One woman
told how she had hired out as scrub
maid in order to see her baby every
day.

Philadelphia. July l6.-A raid on
104 houses which netted 522 prisoners
stunned the Tenderloin Saturday
night. Among the men and women
gathered in the net were some OF the
most desperate characters in the
country and many persons apparently
of respectable families.


Hearings began before Magistrate
Pennock AT midnight Saturday, and
continued without cessation until late
this afternoon Only twenty women
were discharged.


Professional bondsmen, thieves,
pickpockets and criminals OF all sorts
crowded the police stations where the
hearings were held. while lawyers
fought for the release Of clients and
for the most part lost their cases.


The very bottom Of the underworld
fell out. From IL o'ciock Saturday
night, when the raids began, until late
this afternoon every known rule in
the Tenderloin districts was turned
topsy-turvy There was not branch
of forbidden business that was not
shocked into temporary obedience to
the law.


Saturday night 300 policemen, in
squads VI ltH' tdNH uuN'i "a ND'h
mander, assembled at City Hall.
About $50 warrants were issued deslg-
mating the houses TO be raided, and
each squad received an allotment. At
II sharp the squads moved, and soon
the excitement began.


All the territory between Seventh
and Broad Streets, Broad and South
streets. was in a turmoil. Patrol
wagons changed and skidded about,
policemen hammered on doors and
burst their way into houses, and ex-
cited men and women ran about the
streets, not knowing what was going
to happen next or where.


SO many wagonloads Of men and
women were taken to the various po-
lice stations that all the stations were
soon full Then they began placing
the unwilling guests upstairs in the
policemen's quarters until crowded.


Outside the station houses great
crowds gathered. These crowds re-
mained all night and to-day, and were
there as evening fell. watching the
prison vans cart women and men
away.


Sentences varied from ten to thirty
days up the river" and fines from
$40 and costs up. Many were held
in bail for court.

ceded the sinking of the vessel. The
German commander gave orders that
the American flag should be lowered

them into effect. They met with stub
born resistance on the part of the

who refused to haul down the colors,
saying that if the ship had to be sunk
it would be with the flag flying.


capt. Duffy maintained his ground
and so rapidly were the preparations
to sink the Chemung made that further
discussion about the flag ceased, and
after the captain and crew had been
taken aboard the submarine a torpedo
and three shells sent against the side
Of the American ship put her to the
bottom

German commander. Capt. Duffy and
his men had some measure of satisfac-
ton in seeing the flag at the masthead
as the waves firally engulfed their
ship.

The first scattering returns from va
rious sections Of the country shattered
the cocksure confidence which had char
acterized Democratic National Head
quarters since the beginning of the
Presidential campaign. As early as 8
o'clock the Wilson leaders began 70
wear an expression Of doubt and worry,
which was not dispelled by the brave
statements issued from time TO time by
Chairman Vance c. Mccormick from
his private Office, where he was closeted
during the entire evening with Demo-
cratic leaders.


At midnight, when the election of
Hughes had been announced from near
ly all parts of the country, Chairman
Mccormick still claimed victory for
President Wilson, and issued the fol-
lowing statement:


Our reports received up TO mid
night show that President Wilson has
received certainly go electoral votes,
not including Massachusetts and Con-
necticut, nor California and other
western states yet to be heard from"


This statement was supplemented by
another one issued by Mr.. Mccormick
at 1890, as follows:


"The latest returns show that Will
son will have not less than 273 cleo
toral votes.


"Since midnight have received re-
turns showing that Delaware was car
ried by a safe majority. The Demo
cratic state ticket is elected"


The Delaware information came TO
United States Senator Willard Sails
bury. of that state. Senator Salisbury,
who is chairman of the Democratic Sen
atorial Committee. said that the claim
of the Republicans that they would con-
troll the next Senate was absurd. He
also declared that the returns up to
midnight showed that the Democrats
had lost only two Senators and gained
four.


The figures on which he based this
statement, Senator Salisbury added, did
not include the two Democratic candi-
dates of Indiana, where the result was
in doubt.


Soon afterwards, Robert W. Wooley,
director of publicity, said he was prac-
tically certain of 1913 electoral votes
for Wilson. Mr.. Wooley claimed the
following states:


Alabama, Arizona. Arkansas. Cali
fornia, Colorado, Delaware, Florida,
Georgia, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky,
Louisiana, Maryland. Minnesota, Miss
issippi Missouri, Montana, Nebraska,
Nevada, New Mexico. North Carolina,
North Dakota, Ohio. Oklahoma, Oregon,
South Carolina, South Dakota, Tonnes
see. Texas. Utah, Virginia, Washington,
West Virginia and Wisconsin.


But even these eXtravagant claims
did not suffice to lift the fog of gloom
which had settled over the headquar-
ters earlier in the night. Terse bulle-
tins, which flashed from time to time
over the wires from various sections
of the country. were sadly at variance
with the confident words of Mr.. McCor-
mick and Mr.. Wooley.


While Mr.. Mccormick and other
Democratic leaders were issuing their
optimistic statements, the air OF doubt
in the headquarters grew more serious.
The figures compiled by the chiefs APP
parently did not convince the Wilson
followers, who crowded the headquar-
tiers.

London, Aug. 6.-The second great
Turkish thrust at the Suez Canal, of
which so much was expected in Con-
stantinople and the capitals Of the Cen
tral Powers, has been smashed by the
British commander, General Sir Archi-
bald Murray.


The German Offered Turkish army
Of $4,000 swept west along the Medi
terranean coast last Thursday, pushed
beyond Katia in the following twenty
four hours and by Saturday had flung
the British troops back TO Romani.
twenty-five miles from Port Said. In
thirty-six hours they advanced nearly
eight miles.


Late Friday the British resistance
stiffened. The right flank of the Otto
man columns was caught under the fire
of Allied warships in the Bay Of Tina,
and the British land forces took advan-
tage of the confusion in the enemy's
ranks. The Turks were checked for the
time being.


A strong frontal attack on General
Murray's army was then made by the
Turks, and while the British were en-
gagged in rolling back this wave Turk
ish detachments worked their way
around the southern flank. The Brit
ish gave way before both frontal and
flank assaults. Then the British COM
mander ordered the mounted Australian
and New Zealand troops TO give way.
The enemy, interpreting this as a sign
of British demoralization, swung for
ward in hot pursuit.


Before they could realize the danger
the Ottoman forces along the whole
southern wing became involved in the
sand dunes General Murray sprung
the trap. The British forces along the
entire line jumped to the attack.


The Turkish lines halted, wavered,
and then broke. The Anzacs fell on
their rear and the retreat became
rout. More than $500 unwounded
Turkish and German prisoners were
swept behind the British ranks, includ-
ing many German ofhcers. Guns were
abandoned by the score. The pursuit
by the British is continuing.


The British report on the Suez fight
says:


'The general officer commanding in
chief in Egypt reports under date Of
August 5, 11:l5 p. m, the following
further details of the fighting in the
vicinity of Romani on August 3:


THE enemy made frontal attack
on the British intrenchments, in con-
junction with flank attack around
the southern flank, employing $4,000
men and heavy howitzers for the
operation.

London, Oct. 13.-Italian success on
the Carso continues to grow. Slowly
but without pause, Cadorns's troops

resistance.

prisoners, while the Austrians captured
300. Losses on both sides are ex-

damage to the subway station at One

threw the ticket agent and chopper"

light in the station, broke the glass in

in the streets above the station.

press the belief that the bomb was placed
to explode while train was passing and
thus block the tracks.

South.

Newport News, Va, Aug. 19.-Mrs.

sponsor for new steel passenger and
freight steamer of the Mallory Line
launched here to-day. As the big ship
slid down the ways it was christened
Henry r. Mallory, a name that has
been linked for nearly eighty years
with the American merchant marine.


Built for the New York-Texas trade,
the new ship has the general appear
ance of a transatlantic liner, with
superstructure and deck houses amid
ships, leaving large open decks fore
and aft. She is 439 feet in length, 81
feet beam and "a feet deep. There are
accommodations for 100 first class and
100 second class passengers.


The Mallory Line announces that the
Henry r. Mallory, and other boats re-
Gently launched, are the first of big
feet to carry the trade Of the South
west.


Officials of the Mallory Line said the
launching of their recent ships marked
the opening OF new chapter in Amer
lean merchant marine history, pointing
out that for the first time in half a
century the United States Is not only
building more shipping than any other
country, but, during 1916, will probably
launch more vessels than the rest OF
the world combined.

Within, the masters desk is seen,
Deep SCARED by raps official;
The .warping floor, the battered seats,
The ack-knfe's carved initial.
The charcoal frescos on its wall;


Its doors worn sill, betraying
The feet that creeping slow to school,
Went StOrming out to playing!
Long years ago winter sun


ShOne over it at setting;
Lit up it's western window-panes,
And low caves icy fretting.
It touched the tangled golden curls
And brown eyes full of grieving
OF one who still her steps delayed


When all the school were leaving.
For near her stood the little boy


Her childish favor singled;
His cap pulled low upon face


Where pride and shame were mingled.
Pushing with restless feet the snow
To right and left, he lingered;-
AS restlessly her tiny hands


The blue-checked apron fingered.
He saw her lift her eyes he felt


The soft hands light caressing,
And heard the tremble of her voice,
AS if fault confessng.
I'm sorry that spelt the word;


hate to go above you,
Because, the brown eyes lower fell, -
Because, you see, love you"
Still memory to gray-haired man


That sweet child-face is showing.
Dear girl! the grasses on her grave


Have forty years been growing!
He lives to learn, in LIES hard school,
How few who pass above him
Lament their triumph and his loss,
Like her,-because they love him.

Marseilles. May :. The canal under
the mountain between Marseilles and
the River Rhone, one of the most
notable engineering achievements OF
modern times. was officially opened
to-day. in the presence OF members
Of the Cabinet and other officials, IN.
GLIDING Marcel Sembat, Minister OF
Public Works; Etienne Clemente,'
Minister Of Commerce. and Joseph
Thierry, Under Secretary OF War.


Hitherto Marseilles, although
great port of entry for the Mediter-
ranean. has been walled in from cen
trail France by mountainous ridge
that sweeps entirely around the
northern side Of the city. The canal
pierces this barrier, running for hve
miles in tunnel under a mountain.
II thus links Marseilles with inland
cities, such as Lyons. Avignon and
Valcnce. and puts il in touch with
inland commerce along the Rhone. II
also gives Marscilles a direct water
connection with Havre and the North
Sea.


The canal and its tunnel have been
under discussion for nearly ono hun
bred years. but the actual work was
not begun until 1904 The total
length Of the canal is sixty miles,
and the fve-mile section under the
mountain is seventy-fve feet wide and
seventy feet high.

southwest of the Park City district. Alta,

submits reach attitudes OF Il, 800 feet

timber was removed snowslides have
been a menace to life and property.

last Wednesday $40 miles northwest of
Waiting Island.


The steward and one sailor of the

ship, and fears are expressed for the
safety of Captain McGoldrick and eight
Of his crew. who put off in small
boat. but who could not be found by
The Jose. They may have been picked
up by some other ship.


The Jose, bound from Santa Marta

midnight on Friday off the North
Carolina coast, when Captain Ander-
sen sighted them in two small boats.
The seas were running high, but he
picked them up without accident


The Ramos sailed from Philadelphia

coal for Cartagena. Colombia. Two
days later she ran into a tropical
storm. The ship rode the waves in
safety until nearly daylight, when she
sprang a leak and went down in few
hours.


Meanwhile signals Of distress were
flashed and the lfeboats were
launched. Two men were los in this

off and the crew pulled away. Time
was too precious 10 take any supplies.
Ten minutes after the last man left

met the Montenegrin Queen is taken as
evidence of good faith that Montenegro
will cling 70 the alliance with Italy and
the other Entente powers to the end.

AT the last moment Montenegro
preferred national honor and accepted
the guarantees of Italy and her Allies

Investigation will show that the rifles

letic fellow with the bulldog Jaw who

time and hit the bull.

young girls, anxious to be instructed.
The only trouble the instructors had with
them, after getting them to hold the
gun, was to convince them that It was
impossible to hold ones hands over ones
ears and fire the gun at the same time.
And the little scream came every time
the rife barked.

ued silverware that had become hers

afoot in the mountain wilderness trying

Poised there with bended bow?
The roar of the thick-grown jungle
Rises up blurred from below.
The eyes of the beasts are a thousand,
They gleam in the canyons at night;
Their sparkle and stealthy winking
Reflect hot wonder-light
No long leaves make cool their dwellings
No green leaves spread overhead;
The flowers that speckle their lars
Are crimson and sky-red
Full armed they are for the chase,
With close-hid sting and fang;
Their claws are set in iron,


And their law is the law Of the gang.
Huntress, thy bent bow loose,


Let the gold-tipped arrow fly;
Strike the beasts of the wilderness
Spare not to strike till they die.

mony that White, while drunk tried to
kill his mother and sister, all of the

Mrs. White was obdurate. She told Mag
istrate Carson her son was not worth an

expiration of the months sentence he
would come home and harm her.

Lehigh avenues station, made the arrest
yesterday. He was called to the White

lying on couch, clasping a knife. with a

Police of the 26th and York streets sta.

that search along this line will result in
the rounding up of the thieves who raided
the candy and jewelry counters of the Alt.
man Five-and-Ten-Cent Store, 1901 Sus-
quehanna avenue.


When A. I. Epstein, a clerk, opened the
store this morning, he quickly discovered
that all was not we'll with the establish
ment. The floor was Uttered with candy
and many pounds of gum drops peanut
brittle, molasses taffy and other varieties
of sweets were missing. Glass showcases
were covered with the daubs of sticky
fingers, giving evidence of a wholesale
candy orgy. Fifteen dollars was MISS
ing from cash register, and many
"sparklers" were absent from their Hccus-
toned places In the 10.cent jewelry case.


The looters gained entrance to the
store by crawling UP a rainspout in the
rear and climbing through the window
of storeroom.


"It Is the work of boys" said Samuel
Altman, proprietor. ut looks as though
that, after they had eaten all the candy
they could hold, they had stuffed their
pockets with gum drops and other
sweets"


Acting Detectives Williams and Rich
ardson are making the rounds of homes
In search of "tummy ache" sufferers. This
is the second time that the Altman store
has been robbed within two years.

Paris. June 21.-Corporal Clyde Balls
ley, one Of the latest American aviator
recruits, has received a pilots brevet.
Balsley had terrific baptism OF fire
last Sunday in a battle with three COM
rades against forty German planes. A
majority Of the American squadron
were incapacitated by engine and other
troubles.


Only Balsley, Norman Prince and
Rockwell, with French captain, took
the air under orders 10 proceed over
the German lines. They had hardly
reached the enemy's lines when regu-
lar feet of German planes appeared,
including fifteen new model aviatiks
faster than the Nieuports, with a pas
senger to fire from the rear and sides
in addition TO pilots mitrailleuse for
ward.


The American group singled out one
Of the enemy, who Immediately began
TO drop in spirals. As the Americans
followed him the rest of the enemy
swooped upon them en- masse. The ma
chimes of Balsley and Prince capsized
and fell headlong The French captain,
thinking they were doomed, signalled
Rockwell, "Sauye qui peut." Prince
managed to right his plane a few hun
dred feet from the ground and landed
just behind the French trenches unhurt,
though bullet hole in his helmet and
his riddled machine vouched for the
narrowness of his escape.


Balsley was wounded in the thigh by
an explosive bullet. He was saved by
the straps which held him in his seat.
He fell upside down until near the
ground. when he righted his machine
enough TO escape death, though the
plane was badly smashed.


Balsley, too, was lucky enough TO
land behind the French trenches. Sol
dicrs carried him to a dressing station,
where his wound was found to be not
dangerous. lie will probably resume
flying before long. His exploit was re-
warded by the military medal.


Chapman, whose wound has now
healed, and Rockwell have also been
awarded the military medal. They are
both slated for the Legion of Honor.
They expect to return 10 the front in a
fortnight.

STOCKHOLM, June 21-Thanks to
the indulgence of friendly government
officials and the co-operation of the
British consulate in Stockholm, the diff
ficulties of continuing trade with
America under the new Swedish war
trade act" have. been at least tenn
porarily overcome.
Il This new law specifically prohibits
any one in Sweden from entering into
agreements with foreign powers cover
ing the disposition Of goods imported
into this country, and was cstensibly
retaliatory act against the British
blockade in the North sea- In actual
covered that the law really favored
England and threatened to shut OF all
trade with America


Named Trade Commission.


The Swedish government appointed
"a trade commission to handle all for
eign commerce. and the new war trade
act authorizes this commission to
make agreements with foreign govern
CoAiuitiohS- Hc
principle behind these conditions was
that a belligerent nation, in exporting
goods, had a perfect right to demand
the promise that none of such goods
should fall into the hands of an enemy
country. Thus the commission has not
hesitated to extend such promises to
Great Britain covering goods imported
by Sweden from English merchants.


But the Swedish government holds
that Great Britain has no right under
any pretext of international law to
demand guarantee from Sweden COW
ering goods imported into this coun-
try from another neutral country

Britain absolutely refuses to let any
goods pass into Sweden or any other
scandinavian country from the United
States or any other place without
this specific guarantee.

Baltimore, Sept 26.-For more than
twelve hours-from early yesterday after
noon to early this morning-Adrian Dues
berg, the 7-year-old son of Prof dulles
Duesberg. of Johns Hopkins University,
was kept alive by the pulmotor OF the
Gas and Electric Company. But this arti-
fetal respiration failed to save the child's
life. He died shortly before o'clock this
morning from infantile paralysis, which
attacked his respiratory organs and made
natural breathing impossible.


DIR. Duesberg, noted in the medical
profession as an embryolosist and for
merly professor of embryology and pa
thoIogy. at Liege, Belgium, said that
everything that medical science could do
to save his little sons life was done, but
that the case seemed utterly hopeless
from the time that it assumed its serious
aspect


Adrian was moved yesterday from his
parents home in the Tudor Hall apart
ments, University Parkway, to the Chill
dren's Hospital School, on Green Spring
avenue. To have moved the boy without
providing artificial respiration, the phy-
sicians who attended him said, would
have caused his death within FIVE min
utes. The pulmotor, therefore, was in
stalled in an ambulance, and shortly
after l o clock Adrian was taken to the
hospital school, where the physicians felt
that his life could be saved If salvation
were within the range Of medical science.

The authorized representative of the
British press with the French armies,
writing from Nerdun Saturday last,
says:


'As we came into the town-the first
civilians to reach Nerdun since its
evacuation, the Associated Press repre-
sentative. the representative of the
Russian press and my self-the air was
trembling with the battle raging
around Douaumont. Even five miles
away the noise of the German artillery
was deafening. The storm of pro-
jectiles rained upon the French lines
here exceeds anything ever before
know in warfare.


Practically no small caliber guns
were used by the Germans, and the
main artillery preparation was made
with s-inch and 12-inch guns. They
used their heavy guns exactly AS the
French use their 75's. which fire twen-
~ shots minute. In one place, on a
front of 1000 yards with IL depth of
500 yards. $4,000 big shells fell in six
hours. The trenches were literally
swept out of existence. Throughout
the assault here the Germans followed
the plan of concentrating their guns
first on the French left and then grad
ually moving the direction Of their
fire toward the French right"

The fat and pompous manager OF o
big restaurant in Broadway's wholesale
district was standing beside the cash
ier's desk yesterday afternoon when

back his coat and showed badge.


Inspector from the Health Depart

Everything's all right here. I've been

The inspector turned toward the

inside the fairly cool and clean

The Health Department man glanced

That's right" agreed the manager.

spector."

good"

rant on Broadway received the disap-
pointment of his life when supervisor

thing was in such perfect condition





that the manager had visions OF re-
eeiving the first good" mark. But they

Will Put in Screens.

Standish, Mich, Dec 25.-Threer trap
pers. Charles Leonard. George Weston,
and Bert Parker. have reached here from
a hunting trip in the Lake Superior re-
gion and told of a race for lives with a
wolf pack while returning from their
traps last week. The men were on skates
three miles from the nearest cabin when
the wolves appeared.


On of the trappers fired his rife when
the pack approached them and the wolves
quickly tore one Of its wounded members
to pieces, giving the hunters time for a
start.


Several times when the wolves were
nearly on them this was repeated, the
men said, until they finally escaped.

The subway's open ventilating sys-
tenn proved troublesome again yester-
day afternoon, when the dust and ref
use in the open fan troughs at Brook
lyn Bridge station caught fire from an
overheated blower, pouring dense,
sufocating cloud Of steam and smoke
INTO the station.


The accident occurred a few minutes
before o'clock, just as the Saturday
afternoon crowds were rushing for
trains. but traffic was not interrupted.
The trains plouehed through the heavy
smoke. with their passengers climbing
over one another i'm their efforts TO see
the source OF the nre. The smoke pene-
trated through the tubes as far north
as Canal Street, and south TO Wall
Street.


The blaze started in the fan box at
the extreme east Of the station. A
journal became overheated, firing the
waste that has for months been drop
ping into the fan troughs from the
open gratings above. The fire did not
blaze briskly, but smouldered slowly,
giving off a heavy cloud of smoke. On
the west platform Of the station the
fan system is cooled by water. As the
sheet iron ventilating boxes became
heated steam formed where the hot
pipes ran into the cold water. adding
another element 20 the smoke-charged
atmosphere.


The fan was stopped as soon as the
fire was discovered. Within quarter
OF an hour the station. heated by the
pipes and the steam. had become as hot
as furnace. Fremen climbed into
the burning fan troughs to turn their
streams Of water upon the burning
dust. They emerged at short inter-
walls. with their clothing wringing wet.


Police reserves refused to allow pas
sengers to lnger on the station plat
forms. It was more than an hour
after the FIRE broke out before the
smoke and steam had cleared away.

Tomorrow morning. after breakfast, the
last group Of mothers and children to en-
joy Camp Good win:fo this season. will
leave after a stay of two weeks. Tents
will be struck by the camp workers and
stored away, and by Thursday or Friday
but little evidence will be left to show
what busy spot the camp site has been
for the past two months.


Yesterday was uneventful. Religious
services were held in the evening, the
mothers, children and camp workers par
ticipating. The children were sent to
Sunday school as usual in the morning
and the boys of the camp had their Gus
tomary hike. The day was sort of case
of ''the day after the night before" when
the men from the navy yard entertained
the children with big eats and music.
The children were given an opportunity
to rest up from the excitement Of Friday
and Saturday to prepare for the work OF
leaving camp.


Declares Camp a Great Success.


Miss Margaret Simpson, superintendent
of the camp, declared that from point of
view of pleasure, at least, the camp was
a great success this year. All the mothers
and children who visited this year seemed
happy and regretted leaving when their
turn came. Miss Simpson praised the
cooperative spirit of all the mothers who
have stayed at the camp, saying they al
ways were ready and willing to help out
in whatever work came up.


Four groups of mothers and children of
$50 each have been guests at the camp
for two weeks each this year. The last
group has enjoyed the best weather, ac-
cording to Miss Simpson, although some
of the past few nights have been almost
too chilly for out-of-door sleeping.


Members of the Staff.


This year the staff assisting Miss Simp-
son was composed of Misses Elizabeth
Callison and Bessie Lineback, who had
charge of the girls, and Carlton Taylor
and Stephen Baldwin, who had the boys
of the camp under their care. The last
group of volunteer workers was composed
of Misses Schiffman, Dorothy Jacobs and
Elsie Keneaster, who assisted with the
girls. DIR. Berry of Brightwood worked
at intervals among the larger boys, and
Miss Alma Barker. a member of the Girl
Scout organization, helped the camp
workers among the younger ones.


Camp Pleasant also will close tomorrow,
but the baby camp near Camp Good Will,
will remain open indefinitely.

Sir: In your editorial about the
Dutch East Indies you said that Japan
wanted to possess, sooner or later
those Dutch colonies. Without preju-
dice, | believe this not to be Japan's
design.


The Dutch East Indies have pop
ulation Of 55,OOO,0OO. Among them
YOU will find perhaps one thousand
Japanese, principally merchants and
a few planters. Two years ago there
vera no more than 500 Japanese to
be found throughout the Dutch Archi-
pelago. Why? Because the Javanese'
the Malay and Chinese are WORKING
on sugar. rubber, tea and coffee plan
,ations for 40 cents (Holland money!;
thi, is IS cents american money!
nor working day Of twelve hours. The
Japanese don't like to work for such
n small amount, especially not wneh
they emigrate. ~


When railroads are built you Will
see sometimes Japanese as foremeh'
I saw them busy as carpenters, track
LAYERS and with general railroad work
in the Sumatra forests. However
they are exceptions, Chinese, Java
nese and Malay people being generally
foremen. carpenters and track-lsyerS,
If course the more intelligent OF them
As storekeepers, as merchants, tney
are successful, but not in marked
degree, because the largest stores ana
warehouses of Asiatics are in the
hands of Chinese.


II is true the Japanese are export
inc very much merchandise IN the
last few years to the Dutch Eas.
Indian Archipelago, but they VIII
never settle themselves in great num-
bers among the Javanese and Chinese;
certainly not in Java, because its
population of 35,ooO,000 souls Is very
dense. You may travel throughout
Java and you will meet only few
Japanese in Batavia, Bandoung'
Djocja and Sourabaja and few else
where. In Sumatra you will find small
colonies Of japanese in Medan and
Padang. where they have some beau
tiful stores. Nevertheless they have
10 easy task to compete with the
clever and experienced Cinnamon, or
rather Indo- Chinese, because they are
for the greater part halfbloods.


The japanese with some capital pre-
fer TO establish themselves, when they
emicrate, in countries where people
have greater buying power than the
Javanese or Malay. These latter
ignore the value of money and pos
scss very rarely any capital.


Consequently their buying power IS
small They are used to buying in
Chinese stores, because the Chinese
toxic keeper knows how to deal with
them. The native customers will get
all kinds of credit. The Javanese will
buy clothes or something else and
they will pay dime or two every
month until the debt is paid.


The Chnaman will even take the
trouble of cashing the dues himself
every month and will walk for miles
and miles around the country visit
ing the customers. Who else will take
the trouble except the chinese ana
Hindu and Bombay merchants to col
lect their dues with a patience which
extends sometimes over years?


Now, | believe l have explained In
some way why Japanese don't go to
the Dutch East Indian Archipelago.


Turkey lost, during the last Balkan
war, some territory, and it is possible
that agents from Turkey are travel
ling through the country trying to
cause discomfort. There are some
classes of intelligent Javanese and
Malay who want self-government
autonomy, but they realize that if
they insist upon it now they will fall
into the hands of some other foreign
power. If they have to choose they
are all for the Dutch system, and
prefer it above all other colonial sys-
tens.


o. G. THODEN VAN vELZEN.


New York, Nov. ., 1915.

Sir: Woe to those malicious and turbulent
Americans on the border who think and speak

dren slain their property ruined-they have

their own price; and that the President is the
tool of these interests.


They say that Carranza and Villa though
rivals heretofore. are now playing into each
others hands with common hatred against
the ravisher Of their country.


Oh, but it is terrible that such people are
allowed to live! They interfere with Will
sons plans.


But what are Wilson's plans?

From the London Chronicle.


The American party names, "repub-
lican" and democrat" seem to convey
distinction without difference to the
English mind. As with other party
names, however, their significance may
be extricated from their history. The
original Republicans" were actually
the ancestors of the present democrats
Jeffersons party appropriated to them
selves the name of republicans" sug-
gesting that the federalists were anti
republican. The federalists then nick
named the Jefferson party demo-
Gratis" and the hostile nickname, as
with our own whig and tory. was
eventually adopted with pride by the
Jeffersontans themselves. Meanwhile
the federalists were long known as
wings. The modern republican party
deliberately adopted its name when the
various anti-slavery sections coalesced
in Lincoln's time.

Leon, but the line which crosses the
Rio Grande at Brownsville runs west
from Matamoros through Tamaulipas,
Nuevo Leon and Coahuila, turning to
the southwest at Torreon and extend
ing through the state of Durango.

Dolly Lorraine, who has recovered her
sight entirely at Mercy Hospital, joins

careful. She learned from a chorus girl

was a matrimony epidemic among the
chorus girls.

OF the chorus, would marry Carl Open
heimer, a travelling salesman, on Satur-
day, and that Cecil Cotter. another
chorus girl, would be married today to
William Kinley, also of the chorus The
letter states that there have already
been four marriages since the show was
put on the road.

this afternoon. She has recovered her
sight completely. A number Of members
of the local theatrical fraternity called

On the other hand, Harvard had only two

advantage in weight. experience and skill

odds told another story. They favored
Harvard-and logically. For past expert
ence supported the assumption that the
Harvard coaches would be able to weld
their raw material into an offensive and
defensive machine capable of showing
sufficient margin of superiority over
Princeton's.


To establish that superiority required
longer and stronger pull than had been
necessary at Harvard for many years.

veterans invincible and even her unpromis-
ingly green teams victorious.

To the Editor of The Tribune.


Sir: The public places the blame of the
recent mobilization on the regular army
1t apparently ignores the fact that the regu-
lar army is made up of two distinct parts
first, the fighters; second, the swivellers, and
that even these must be judged by their acts
the goats separated from the sheep, the
workers from the red tapers.


The country has ever been exutant over
cur fighting regular and his immediate SUI
perior. They have carried the flag from the
Atlantic to the Pacific, from Niagara to Mex
leo, always with honor to themselves and
glory to the United States. The man behind
the gun is loved and respected by all, he is
the meat and bone of the army.


Now we come to the swivellers of the War
Department. They must be divided into the
workers and the red tapers. The workers
gave US the canal, our guns and our ammu-
milton, made victory possible.


But the red tapers! What did they do
They swivel and swivel and swivel out red
tape. They cannot rise above the red tape
Of their making. They are hopelessly behind
the times in common sense foresight, mod
ern business methods. The lessons from the
past have no meaning for them. The prob
lens of the future they do not face or can
not solve. But the red tapers know that to
work pull and keep it well oiled beats mill
tary efficiency They are the maggots on
the army meat. Without wandering far
afeld the red tapers might go to the Navy
Department and learn how to care decently
for the army dead, try to grasp the way the
navy transfers the bodies of our sailors and
marines from Vera Cruz to the New York
Navy Yard, and learn how the Presi-
dent could speak quite near the collins con-
tanning the men who followed the flag to
their eternal rest.


We certainly need promotion by elmina-
ton. Will Congress wake up and investigate
the red tape maggots?


MCOSKRY BUTT.


New York, Aug. IS, 1916.
headline:
THE BREED OF SWIVELLERS

Blame Rests Upon the Red Tapers of the


War Department.

Dull mortals who cannot sec beyond
their own short noses may dismiss Tody
Hamilton as plain liar. Let them, and
welcome. The particular magic of which
Tody was ringmaster is not for staked-out
clods. Such imponderable substances as
Joy and humor were his working material
and the American sky was his limit. AS
we'll apply a yardstick to the Milky Way
as talk of facts in the same breath with
spangles and elephants and the magic saw
dust ring.


A great clown, best describes him.
though he never stepped from behind the
scenes. His was the imagining of mar
velous hoaxes, the distilling Of adjectives
that never were on sea or land, the splash
ing of the great American circus tent with
coors that still amaze and cheer. There
might have been circus without Tody
Hamilton. But what mute, inglorious
thing it would have been


Other press agents come and go. ALTER
alton, snatched from the clouds, lives on
as the slave of blurbing magazine editors.
Other days, other adjectives. But Tody is
gone; the comedy is ended. We can only
hope that each year, munching peanuts
rapturously while Coralie hangs by her
pink legs somewhere between sawdust and
heaven, faint echoes of the thrilling, ire
mendous, tantalizing past will not fail to
return and bless us.

NORFOLK, August 3.-Some-
where out in the Atlantic today
the big German Submersible
Deutschland probably is journey
ing safely homeward after hav-
ing successfully run the allied
warships' blockade off Cape
Henry last night The giant
undersea craft submerged a mile
off the coast shortly before 9
O'Clock. and in so far as is known
here, she was unobserved by any
OF the allied warship patrol
which had been guarding the
capes against her escape for sew
eral weeks.


At Cape Henry today one two
funnel warship was visible. lying
out beyond the three mile line.


One of the last acts of Capt. Koenig
and his crew. according to Capt Hinsch
of the tug Timmins. which acted as her
convoy from Baltimore to the capes,
was to stand on the deck of the sub
mersible and give three rousing cheers
for America and the American people.


The final dash of the Deutschland to
the sea was virtually without incident
Eighteen miles Chesapeake bay. at
the crossing of the Old Point and cape
Henry channels. she began to gather
speed about sundown last night. and
In little over two hours was plung-
ing along under the surface of the At
lantic. With only a slight delay after
reaching the capes, she dashed into the
sea and submerged. Only one warship.
q United States torpedo boat destroyer.
was sighted by the submersible in her
entire trip from Baltimore, Capt
Hinsch declared.

crew. On The way the Venezuela will
call at Cardiff, Santos and Rio Janeiro.

dor and Colombia. They will leave
shortly for San Francisco after being
refitted.


The Dutch vessels purchased by the
Pacific Mail Steamship Company were
constructed last year. The Venezuela
and Colombia are of $500 gross tons
each and $50 feet long and were built
in Amsterdam. The Ecuador is Of 5000
tons and was built in Flushing.


Last August the Pacific Mail Com
pany sold the five largest vessels of its
oriental feet to a subsidiary corpora
tion of the International Mercantile
Marine. The vessels were the Man
churia, Mongolia, Korea, Siberia and
China.

H. NJ. S. Frauenlob must be definitely

Although the weather was unfa-

and by the speed with which they
acted"

The first naval battle on a grand scale

highly satisfactory to the Germans,

man commentators assert, by the res

London, Aug. 1.-THE Italians have
cleared the way for an advance on
Trieste along the railroad skirting the
gulf.


In a series Of brilliant attacks they
have conquered the whole of the Do
berdo plateau, taking by storm the
strongholds of San Martino del Carso
and Rubbia.


South of Gorizia the lsonzo bends
sharply to the west, forming a deep
salient between Gorilla and Monfal-
cone. This wedge made dangerous an
advance from either point, for the flank
of the advancing army laid itself open
to attack.


The Italian plan contemplates two
movements eastward, one along the
railway running from Gorizia through
st. Daniel and the other along the
coastal road from Monfalcone TO
Trieste. The advance from Monfalcone
has been held up for more than seven
months because of this flank threat.


Austrian Salient Wiped Ont.


When Gorilla fell the Duke Of Aosta
began the clearing of the Carso plateau,
on which lay the Austrian wedge For
three days the battle has Continued,
until finally the Austrian salient has
been completely dislodged and the line
between Gorilla and Monfalcone
Strengthened. The Teutons have fallen
back TO the line of the VALERIE.


This victory makes it possible for
the Italians to begin an advance along
the coast without Danger to their flank.
While one army IS battling for the
heights east of Gorilla another can
begin the march from Monfalcone,
forcing two wedges into the Austrian
line that will squeeze the enemy out
of the Carso plateau. When this has
been accomplished the road for an In
vasion Of interior Austria will be open.


Behind Gorilla the battle continues
with unceasing fury. The Italian cav
airy and cyclists are driving the Aus
trians from the valleys east OF the
fortress city. The Teutons are retreat,
ing along the railway line toward
Dornberg and striving to reform their
line in that neighborhood.

third soon after. which dropped into

swung out. the crew Of forty-two and
the four hostlers donned life pre-
servers and the ship put on full speed.

sighted at any time, owing partly to
weather conditions, and the officers of
the Siamese Prince were unable to say
whether their vessel was pursued The
hostlers included great many Ameri-
cans, it was stated.

miles at sea, while heavy sea was
running. No attempt was made to
torpedo the ship, which is owned by
Furness. Witty & Co. and which car
ried no passengers. The officers Of the
vessel judged that the attacking boat
was about mile distant.

tomorrow they will be sent back to the

been treated best by the weather man
says Miss Margaret Simpson, superin-

so cold that every blanket in the
camp was used.


Camp Good VIII started in a small

then there have been children and
mothers at Washington's charity
fresh air camp. This is the usual
time for the camp to close. as the
nights in the latter party of August
sometimes are unpleasantly cold for
outdoor sleeping.

Z CINCINNATI, January 1.-Richie

this afternoon. The bout went the

bone. Thereafter the now Of claret was

chief second for the champion, while

Both men spared cautiously at the

Kiibane took the third round easily.
He led with vicious right uppercut, and

Mitchell came back strong in the fourth.

London, July 21.-Driving the
Germans back over the same ground
from which they launched their
great counter attack early in the
week, the British last night forced
them through the Foureaux wood,
on the crest Of the Albert plateau.
A counter attack in which gas
shells and bombs were used won
back portion of the wood, but the
British held the southern half
against the most violent assaults,
and tonight are preparing to seize
the rest of the position.


AT the same time German counter
attacks against the positions won by
the French yesterday south of Soye-
court were thrown back with heavy
losses, and General Foch's men spent
the day almost unmolested in consol-
idating their new lines.


Germans Admit Loss.


The German official statement to-
night admits the loss of three kilo-
metres of first line trenches south
Of Hardicourt, but makes no men,
tion of other actions. 1t states that
the Allies used 100000 men in the
I Thursday attacks, and says their 4
maximum gain was 500 yards. A
little ground was gained, the Brit
ish admit, by a German drive at
the northern edge of the Leipsic
salient, south of Thiepval, but it
was quickly won back. No effort

press the attack around Verdun.

the Germans are bringing masses Of
troops from Verdun and guns from
ether points, in an endeavor to stem
the Allied advance. Meantime, the
indications are that the Allies are

failed.

Haig was able to push the German
nne back in the same place where
their counter offensive had been

Berlin, July 19.-Reports from the
southeastern front indicate that the
Russians, after fortnight of compare
tive inactivity, have brought up heavy
reinforcements of infantry and cavalry
and have now resumed strong aggres-
sive on the headwaters of the Moldava,
near the Hungarian frontier.


A change in the weather has facili-
tated the operations, after clear, hot
weather, in which it was impossible to
conceal the movements of troops for
sudden attacks in great force. The
Russians are showing the utmost ten
acity, and their artillery is playing an
important role in the operations.


The Austrian mountain batteries,
however, have achieved splendid results
against it. The Russians prepare only
hasty field positions. believing that the
Austrian resistance can soon be broken,
but, the reports say. the Austrian in
fantry is withstanding all the attacks
and filing the ground in front Of the
trenches with Russian dead.


The correspondents intimate that the
time is approaching when the Austrians
will assume the offensive and try to
roll back the Russian tide.

BERLIN, Jan. II (by maiD.-The Ger
man censorship was roundly denounced

criticisms were being made, the heads OF
the foreign office. which is. responsible

tary news, were at the Reichstag listen

American correspondents, except that
the Socialists are much more bitter
They charge the censorship with dis
elimination, citing instances where some
journals have been permitted to dis
cuss peace, while the Socialists have
not.

much worse with the organisation

the restrictions about food discussions.
especially the butter shortage, were too
severe and one publisher said the
newspapers were losing thousands OF
dollars because so mucn news is sup

correspondents Is that they are so re-
stricted by the censorship that In writ,

they wish, but what they think the
censor will pass. Recently the, corre-
spondents discovered that their own ac-
counts OF theNbutter shortage and the
demonstrations in Berlin were suppress
ed while the government wireless sent
a denial that there were riots In Berlin.


American correspondents also believe
that the government is too strict about
preventing comment on current news
affecting the relations between the
United States and Germany. Most cor
respondents, for instance. were prohib-
tied from sending anything about the
recall Of Captains Won Papen and Boy
Ed.


on the whole. the censorship appears
to be growing less liberal.

Chatham, N. j., July 2s.-Two boys
and two girls were shot over the spill
way Of the dam and drowned here to-day
when their canoe upset. One girl waa
rescued after she had clung for ten
minutes TO a branch Of an overhanging
tree.


The drowned are Mary Dowd. six
teen years old, and her brother, Edwin,
fourteen, of Madison, N. j.; William
Duffy. sixteen, of Madison, and Eliza
beth Getz, fourteen, of Philadelphia.
Margaret Hinch is the only member OF
the canoe party who was rescued


With others from Madison they
started out to-day for the Old Mill, a
favorite picnic ground half way De-
tween Summit and Chatham, where a
dam broadens the Passaic River. Ordi-
narily the water is calm above the
dam. but to-day the Passaic was many
feet above it's normal level.


Gates Had Been Opened.


The fioodgates Of the dam had been
opened to carry off the water, and Sam
uel Edwards, proprietor of the boat
house, had given orders that no boats
were to be rented. Somehow the pic
nickers from Madison got hold of a
canoe. however, and set out. Their COM
panions watched them from the bank.


They went upstream and kept near
the shore, where the current was not
go swift. All went well. But the water
was full Of tricky little eddies that
pulled the canoe slyly this way and
that, and after a brief paddle the girls
decided they would feel safer ashore.


Coming back with the surge of the
current the canoe gradually increased
its distance from shore, and when the
dam was sighted was almost. IN mid
stream. The boys put forth their best
efforts at the paddles, but despite their
endeavors their craft was caught in the
CLASSY incline that led to where the
Passaic was pouring eight feet deep
through the spillway to the rocks below.


Girls Cry for Help.


The girls began to scream for help
when they saw they were caught in the
grip of the current and the boys
seemed to get new strength from the
terror in their voices. By frantic en-
deavors they managed to veer the
canoe to the left of the ioodgates.


1t brought up quartering against an
abutment of the dam and the upstream
side began TO careen TO the pressure
of the current. Before il went under
however, there was a cracking and the
boat broke in two against the abut-
ment-


The FIVE occupants were swept along
with the fragments of the canoe toward
the spillway and brushed along the
face of the dam, which in places IS over
hung by bushes and tree branches
Miss Hinch succeeded in grasping a
branch that held. She kept her grip,
although the current snapped her out
to full length in jiffy and put tre-
mendous strain on her arms


Boy Grasps Branch.


Edwin Dowd also managed to get
grip on a tree branch. The others were
rolled over and over, sometimes above
and sometimes below the surface, with
small chance Of seizing anything. one
by one they were pulled into the last
oily black stretch, where the water
fairly Kissed as it rushed smoothly
toward the fall.


Dowd was nearer the foodgates than
Miss Hinch, and she could watch hlm,
ss well as their companons. She saw
the bush 20 which she was holding had
been undermined by the water and was
gradually losing its grip on the earth;
There was nothing to which she could
transfer her grasp, and she did not
dare warn him Of the new danger, lest
he let 20 in his fright or make some
sudden movement which would tear his
support entirely away.


Men about the boathouse had seen
the plight of the canoeists and were al
ready on the way to help them. Three
had been swept through the foodgates
before they arrived. Joseph Herberger

NEW YORK, October 10.-The
French liner Espagne came into port
today with an exciting story of her ex-
perience Sunday night and Monday,
when lifeboats were swung out and all
precautions taken for an encounter
with the German submarine raider.
First word reached the Espa gne Sum
day by wireless that the German raider
was at work in nearby waters. All pre-
cautions were Immediately taken, but
only the officers of the ship were aware
of the danger. though the precaution-
airy measures as soon gave the pas
sengers an inkling of the facts The
course of the Espagne was changed
sh1rply to the southwark. She had been
heading about due west expecting to
reach New York Monday, but the course
southwest heightened her voyage another
twelve to fifteen hours. All lifeboats
were swung clear from deck and
cleared for any emergency. Numbers in
the lifeboats had previously been as
signed to passengers while crossing the
war zone outside Bordeaux, and each
passenger had a ticket designating the
number of his lifeboat and the COM
mander.





upper deck astern was cleared for action.
All passengers and crew were perfectly
calm during the preparations. and there
was the usual gayety. though some of the
woman passengers kept their lifebelts
conveniently near them. Mme Sarah
Bernhardt. Lima Cavalieri and the other
distinguished artists aboard heard and
discussed the reports, but showed no
evidence of anxiety


Through Monday the Espagne zigzagged
in her course. She was so far 3outh---I40
miles from her usual course--that pas
sengers thought she might make Ches-
apeake bay. Monday night the ship
trembled as full speed was put on, and
the zigzag course was pursued. Many
remained on deck late at night. but no
hostile craft was seen. The ship finally
reached the three limit. within
which sanctuary she stayed for the rest
Of her voyage

morning the passengers gathered In the
first class saloon and signed testimonial

appreciation Of the judgment OF the COM

Her face and hands were cold, and
Kazan muzzled them tenderly. Her eyes
were closed. He snuggled up close
against her, with his ready jaws turned
toward the dead man. Why was she so
still. he wondered?


A long time passed, and then she
moved. Her eyes opened. Her hand
touched him.


Then he heard n step outside.

thrill of fear-fear of the club-he went
swiftly to the door. Yes, there was his

ly, almost falling at each step, and his

grief rose and died softly in his throat.

Washington, Oct. 24.-No report or
the fight in Santo Domingo had reached
the Navy Department tonight, but off,
cials assumed that the latest outbreak
was the work of small band of rebels
who recently revolted from the Do
minican army and that it did not
presage any general attempt at dis
order.


Last reports from the island told OF
comparative quiet throughout the re-
public, where the American marine
forces are busy organizing the native
constabulary which is to police the
country under the direction of Ameri-
can officers.


Captain William W. Low was sent to
Santo Domingo with his company from
the Marine Barracks at Philadelphia.
He was a native of New Hampshire,
appointed to the Marine Corps from
Connecticut in 1899. and was forty
seven years old. Officers at Marine
Corps headquarters tonight were un-
able to identify the name Atwood.


There has been little trouble in the
Dominion Republic since early July,
when the United States marines occu-
pied the principal ports of the island
and crushed the Aras revolution. Dur
ing the three months previous there
had been constant conflicts.


President Jiminez had resigned early
in the spring TO prevent American in
tervention. General Arias. leader OF
one of the anti-American factions.
seized the city of Santo Domingo.
American marines were landed and he
was driven out of the city, but he con-
tinued his activities in the Interior


American marines were then sent IN
strong force to the island and spread
overland. occupying Monte Cristi,
Puerto Plata, Santiago and lie vega.
Scores of skirmishes took place be
tween the opposing forces, III when
some 100 Dominicans and one ofhcer
and three marines of the United States
were killed.


On July 3 a sharp engagement took
place between the American marines
and the rebels near Santiago. The
same day Admiral Caperton, command
ing the United States forces, pro-
claimed martial law and virtually took
over the affairs of the island republic.


After that there was but one serious
disturbance, on July 6, when revolu-
tionists attacked the American forces
at Santo Domingo. Twenty-seven rep
els were killed, while one marine fell:
Soon afterward Arias capitulated, and
the provisional government. under Gar
yaial. assumed control of afalrs.

ering their mistake. the black birds
began to make war on the butterflies.

Paris, May s.-The tremendous re-
awakening of the Verdun battle is still
broiling. The opposing armies have
tsen necessarily struggling for the
mastery since yesterday afternoon. but
the French have now recovered from
the first shock Of the German ava
lanche and have taken the aggressive
into their own hands.


The constant enemy bombardment
since Friday ceased yesterday at 4 in
the afternoon and down through the
ravine between lie Mort Homme and
Hill S04 poured the German infantry.


But the attack was a double header,
and simultaneously four Prussian regi-
ments charged en- the front between
Haudoumont Farm and the Caillette
Wood on the east side OF the Meuse.
The combined evenings operations are
the greatest offensive delivered by
the Crown Prince since the first at
tacks in March.


The purpose of the left bank assault is
to turn both lie Mort Homme and Esnes.
An entire German army corps rushed
down the ravine between the two hills,
confident that the trenches blocking its
mouth had been demolished by artillery
preparation. At least this was the ex-
PLANTATION for the use Of so great
number. The calculation was correct,
and neither trench nor mitrsilleuses
had been spared by the French gunners
to hinder the German onslaught.


But as the ravine filed to overflow
ing by the forty thousand Germans an
intense she'll fire opened on them. The
French had only one arm left with
which to strike. IL was the artiller-.
and they were using it. This caused
slaughter, which was good payment for
the communication trench which they
had lost.


To-day comes the news that the
"Seventy-fves" held the horde under
control until the infantry reformed
and wrested the communication trench
from German hands. The territory lost
meanwhile in the attack on the left
bank likewise was partially regained.


1t is believed here that the Germans
are attacking thus at Verdun because
they cannot allow the battle to end.
They have such percentage of their
equipment there they cannot permit
the centre OF operations to shift to

The great white plague-tuberculo-

other disease in the United States.

this frightful ailment. To go into de-
tails of the subject is very disgusting.
but disgust will not kill anyone. Con
sumption will. and flies help.


Assuming that bedridden consump-

closed vessels which flies cannot en-
ter, consider the careless consumptive
on the street. He has a coughing
spell, raises germ-laden pus from his
infected lungs and spits into the high
way. Flies Immediately swarm on
this sputum, feed cover their padded,
hairy feet with the stuff and buzz into
the nearest open window or door.

measure. Potatoes went first, in the
belief that the absence of spuds woul
increase the list of honor students.
Twas not to be. So all side dishes

That was the last straw.


Corned beef and cabbage was the
first days menu. When the second

salmon salad. The third day offered
slices of meat, olives and cubes o.
cheese. And then-aye! and then

lasted was the luncheon. Pickles be
gan disappearing from pearby shops
and the proprietors Suddenly saw
visions of much bioated bank accounts

and protested.


We're starving" they said. We've
got TO have more to eat or---or


The ultimatum was carried out last
week When through with the meals
provided by the college the girls
sought bake shops and lunch counters
The "off- -the-campus tea rooms were
swamped with fair diners every noon
Candy stores ordered unusually large
quantities from the manufacturers.
The girls came in more sleepy than
ever.


Authorities at the college decided to
ease up bit. The experiment, which
was supposed TO last a month at least.
was cut short yesterday, when Miss
Eleanor Leslie, president of the senior
class, announced that the old order
Of hearty luncheons would be restored
Immediately.


When the news foated over the
campus it caused an outburst Of re-
joicing almost Unprecedented To-day
the tables were decorated with po-
tatoes and the little sweets that tickle
the palate The shopkeepers wep.
bitterly as their balloon of hope was
punctured.


But, it was learned from authorita-
tive sources, the persons responsible
for the limited diet have not given up
the plan.

The St. Nicholas Skating Rink is all

season Of the Amateur Hockey League.
The persons who do their own skst-
ing on the ice have been thronging the
rink for several weeks now, and tSey
have found numerous improvements
installed since the close of last season.
For one thing. the surface of the ice
is scraped after each skating session,
a real. live horse drawing the scraper.
Joe Hoblitz, head instructor AZ the
rink. sits on the seat and handles the
reins over his spirited charger with the
skill OF Pop" Geers. The new dec
orations are artistic, many colored Lam
terms shedding their light over the ice.
At the western end of the rink, where
the skaters sit on the platform to rest,
a forty-foot cushion has been placed.


But below stairs the greatest trans
formation has been wrought. The en-
tire interior has been made over and
the ST. Nicholas, the Hockey Club Of
New York and the Irish-Amerlcan
teams have their own private club
rooms. Two new organizations, the
Brokers' Skating Club and the Artists
Skating Club. composed OF members OF
those professions, also have private
rooms there, and then for the generai
public, of the masculine sex, there is
an ample locker room, with shower
baths.


Above the rink proper, on the mez-
amin. door at the western end Of the
building. there are rest and locker
rooms FOR women, and comfort Is car
ried almost to the extremes. In TACT,
for such a strenuous sport as hockey,
some of the veteran players are apt 10
consider the new arrangement as
tending to coddling.


The new Kinks opened in New York
City this season are but another evil
dence of the tremendous hold skating
has taken upon the American people.
The movement is nationwide and
shows signs of increasing indefinitely.
John f. Davidson, the professional en-
ployed at the st. Nicholas Rink, re-
turned from Europe last week and re-
ported that the craze had even struck
London, in spite of the war.


Although the British War Depart
ment has taken over nearly every ice
rink in the country for army and navy
uses, the English people skate when
and where they can. mostly at the
aires that have miniature Kinks. Even
members of the nobility have taken up
the sport, and Davidson believes that
as soon as the last shot has been fired in
the war, everybody who has saved two
good legs out of the melee will take to
the steel runners.


In the United States, according to
Davidson, there is hardly a city of
more than 10000 population that has
not its own ice skating rink, all built
within the laat year.

The time honored geraniums or

creasing load of paper. 1.-THE Man
chester Guardian" makes the regret

Cabinet will welcome public discus

press" attacks.


Computations showing an APP
preaching world shortage in food
are alarming. Argentine crop re-
ports are very depressing and ex-
plain the weakness of Argentine
rails. Heroic measures here would
include closing down luxury shops
and luxury manufactures and con-
centration of the productive energy
on articles Of prime necessity. Ris-
ing food prices will greatly raise war
expenditures everywhere.

likely to last is the manufacture of
synthetic drugs. Many enterprising
and clever young chemists have been
working successfully to supply the
market with these hitherto German
monopolies.

fore the war German dolls wigs

as well as the wigs are being manu-

ernment's control, with the result

Two German seamen, who escaped
from internment in Spain and lay snug
ly hidden in the hold of the Antonio
Lopez when British destroyers over
hauled the ship off Gibraltar and
searched II for stowaways, were halted
at Ellis Island yesterday. They were
Franz Wischnewsh and August Halen-
fager, formerly Of the crew of the Ger
man steamer Belgrano, interned at Co.
runna, Spain, at the outbreak of the
war. For the five days they were in
hiding they lived on sea water and
black bread.


Two months ago, the pair said, they
decided they could bear inactivity no
longer, and made a break for liberty.
They lodged their guards and fled to
Cadiz. There they obtained jobs as
longshoremen and helped load the An
tonic Lopez. Although realizing New
York was the next port of call, they hid
in the hold, where they nearl y sufo.
Gated after the matches were battened
down. When discovered, four days
later. they were so emaciated that they
were placed under the doctors care in
the ships infirmary. They were re-
ported to the immigration officials yes
terday morning and were sent 10 Ellis
Island pending the hearing of their
case. The German Consulate and vari-
Gus German societies have offered to
aid them.
