history of athletics at Syracuse Univer'
sity. Although individual Orange aggre-
cations have made better records than
have been made since the opening of col
lege last fall. never have Syracuse teams
accomplished so complete a history of
success


Starting with the football season In 1915
and closing with sensational victory on
the Hudson, the athletic year has been
brimful with honors, and all university
authorities from Chancellor James R.
Day down are elated.


The reception given homecoming oars
men was tremendous. The name of
Charley Whiteside, the phenomenal var
sity stroke, has been shouted from all
corners of the city-the entire municipal
ity having been thoroughly enthused by
the glowing success. Praise for Coach
James A. Ten Eyck has come from city
officials and prominent citizens, gradu-
ates of rival colleges.


Syracuse appreciates the crew victories
because of the limited material with
which Coach Ten Eyck has been work.
Ing. The midseason victories In the New
England cup race In the American Hen
ley, and over the Annapolis add much to
the Syracuse nautical record.

larger

The Point Breeze Motordrome combined
more excitement last night than any time
during its history. The 1OO-kilometer race

part in It formed the magnet that drew
the largest crowd that ever witnessed
race at the famous speed bowl.


Shortly after the race started and with
Ryan leading at the seventh mile all the
lights went out and the vast crowd and
the riders with their pacemakers were in
total darkness.


After delay of 10 minutes the current
came back amid great cheering. During
the darkness the riders had many narrow
escapes from accidents. but good fortune
prevailed and Grassy Ryan the Irish lad,
was the only one who was hurt in mix
up. Both of his legs were badly bruised,
but he gamely continued in the race and
came in second.


Just after the men were sent off to n
new start after the light incident one of
the large arc lamps which hangs over the
track fell with n TERRIBLE crash almost on
top of Stenhouse. who was Ryan's pace
maker.

woman. haggard from a sleepless 24.hour
railway Journey. arrived here late yes.
terday afternoon and went to the little
village Of Pink, lin the mountains Of

missing son was waiting for her to take

Glass, of 13 Lineau place Jersey city,
whose four.year.old boy Jimmy disap.

Penn. Once again she was following one
of the frutless clues which have dragged
her 5000 miles across the United States
since her child vanished She said the
boy at pink was not her son.

roads to Pink At Pink live Mr. and

on May 10, 1915. Jimmy Glass was play

mer home at Greeley. Then suddenly he
was gone. The family searched for him
all that day, but he could not he found.

looking for him ever since


once she Travelled to Oklahoma certain
that the lost boy held there was her son.
Again, she went to South Carolina, sure
that Jimmy would greet her at the end
of her journey. Both times she came back
broken by the disappointment.


Saturday Mrs. Glass left Jersey City
on the old bitter track which has always
led to nothing. Yesterday, as she neared
the place where Holly Ray Farchild"

tain that this time she would find her son.

CHARLESTON, S. c., March IS
With the country full of talk about
foreign trade and the need for i'm
proving the merchant marine and cul-
tivating the business of South America.
the far southern ports of the United
States rise up and demand to be heard.


New Orleans. of course, has a large
and well established business. Charles
ton, Savannah, Jacksonville. Tampa,
Mobile and Pensacola are the ones IN
question. They all have fine harbors
which are free from ice all the year
around; the government has spent
many millions to improve their chan
nels, and the citizens have built and
are building excellent terminal faclli-
ties. They are all dressed up to go TO
the International trade party. but they
have nothing to ride in. Robinson
Crusoe had a fine harbor. but he had no
bottoms That's all that prevented him
from forming a cocoanut trust and get
ting rich.


The southern ports are in the same
fix. They have not the bottoms. mean
ing thereby regular sailings for Tor
eign ports. Therefore they can't get
railroad rates from interior points that
would attract manufacturers to export
via the south instead of the north. II
they had the bottoms they could get
the rates. and vice versa. But. generally
and broadly speaking, they have
neither.

chaufeurs, has infantile paralysis. For
weeks Collender's Point, Noroton and

places, although the owners thems eive,
have been free 70 come and go. In no
place was the quarantine stricter than
at Brick House, the summer home OF
Andrew Carnegie.

in a cottage on the Carnegie premises,
100 feet from the mansion. To-day he
was sent to the contagion ward OF the
Stamford Hospital for treatment for
infantile paralysis. He had not been off
the Carnegie premises since the quar-

text:
Why does the storekeeper wrap up the
goods you buy with needless coveringsf
Because you, the customer, expect your
parcels to be neat in appearance. You
do not want the nature of your purchase
known, perhaps. You want to have your
goods delivered unidentified. Whether
YOU take the parcels home with you or
have them delivered, you want them
covered.


This demand or expectation on the
part of the customers, puts the mer-
chants to a heavy expense in needless
wrappings. He must buy tons Of paper
in the course of the year to meet your
refinements of taste. And you pay the
paper bill You pay more and more for
this paper. as the price rises, owing to
the increased demand and the reduced
supply. You are paying not only more
for the goods you buy, but for the
wrappings that cover them.


Fully half of the paper wrappinss
used in the stores are unnecessary. They
are superfiuous. Paper is wrapped
around cardboard boxes that could just
as we'll. just as neatly and just as safely
be sent home or carried home uncovered.
Articles already wrapped are put within
paper bags, or holding boxes, for con-
venience or concea1ment. These addi-
tional wrappings are not only expensive
and the customer pays the expense
but they delay the service. At this sea-
son, when the shops are beginning to
feel the crowding of Christmas buying,
every bit Of time taken to wrap parcels
unnecessarily is waste. These delays
react upon the counters and make for
lost minutes and hours for stores and
for customers.


The merchants cannot stop wrapping
goods needlessly unless the customers,
recognizing the waste of the old prac-
tice and the economy of simpler deliver
les. express their desire for less closely
covered goods. Why should the Gus
toners be viking to receive their pur
chases with less paper around them:
Because they are thereby contributing to
an economy that will eventually bene-
fit them in lowered store costs, and con-
sequently lower retail prices. By ex
peeting less of needless wrapping the
buyers permit the merchants to institute
reforms that will save both parties much
money in short time.

London. August s.-Foch and Haig
have resumed the combined offensive
along the Somme and again are max
ing steady progress.


The fighting now centres around
Guillemont, a strong position IN the
German second line and on the road
to Combles. While the French are
advancing their line to the south. the
British are pushing slowly eastward


Foch's troops in the last two days
have won a German line north OF the
somme along front Of six kilometres
1878 miles) and to a depth of from
300 to 500 metres. Thus Combles Is
being fanked on the south.


Meanwhile the British. who advanced
their line 400 yards southwest OF
Guillemont to-day, threaten to flank
Combles from the north. Before long
il is extremely likely that the town
will be attacked from two sides. lts
fall will open the way for the inser-
tion of 7 wedge between Peronne and
Bapaume, the first objectiyes OF the
Allied push in Picardy.


French Attacking at Ferdun.


The French, continuing the pressure
along the Somme, have again taken
the initiative in the verdun battle.
Furious fighting continues in this
soc,or hut the Germans. whose attack
last night regained a footing in the
Tbiaumont work, have been halted
again.


Petain has returned to the attack
and besides winning back all the

Thiaumont work. has taken a line of
trenches on the Vaux-Chapitre front
The Crown Prince seems unable to
hold any gains his fierce attacks may
win for him.


The British possession of Pozieres

wedge is now broadening eastward
from the Trones Wood and causing
an increasing menace to Combles. The
Germans are making fierce attempts to

have lost, but all of these efforts have
been frustrated.

Their failure in four attacks north

troops still undaunted. Using flaming
darts, they assailed the British line
here four more times to-day. The first
three attacks were thrown back with
heavy loss, but the fourth succeeded in
penetrating the British trenches along
a fifty-yard front. The battle here is
still in progress.


All the unofficial reports from Haig's
front dwell on the spirit of absolute
elation with which the British troops
are fighting. All are imbued with the
feeling that individually and collec-
lively they are superior to the Ger
mans.


Timing his strokes carefully with
those of his Allies on the south. Haig
is forging ahead northward and east
ward. The Germans defending the re-
naming approaches TO the Albert pla-
teau are exhausting themselves IN coun-
ter attacks. London expects before long
another sharp thrust northward from
Pozieres that will put Msrtinpuich and
Thiepyal in serious peril.

London, Nov. 13.-Haig's troops
have broken through the main Ger
man line west of Bapaume, held by
the Kaiser's forces for two years
and converted into a series OF tas-
tions.


Striking along a five-mile front
on both sides of the Ancre to-day
the British advanced on the whole
line, at points for more than a mile.
and carried by storm the villages CT
Beaumont Hamel and Saint Pierre
Divion. More than 1000 prisoners
already have been passed back.


Thus the battle Of the Ancre has
opened. Slowly the British forces
have been forging northward toward
their objective, Bapaume. But now
they have delivered a blow from tie
west, taking the enemy completely

Failed In first Attempt


The task Haig's men carried
through to success to-day was at
tempted the first time on July !,
when the Somme offensive opened.
At that time the German defences
north of the Ancre proved too strong
and the effort was abandoned. The
British thrust then was made from
the south, in an attempt to outfank
the German position.


With dawn to-day the battle began.
A storm OF shells described as the
most terrific the shrapnel torn Somme
country has yet witnessed burst on the
German defences. The strongest OF
these was Beaumont-Hamel, atop
hill. Further north and little TO the
east is Serre, which also stands high
on a ridge, while to the south OF the
Ancre is st. Pierre Divion, a strong
hold on a height.


This was the work set for the Brit
ish. Deep trenches, winding in dizzy
maze, dugouts bristlng with machine

When the first effort to storm these

WASHINGTON, March s0.-The Com
mercial Exchange OF Philadelphia today
lost It's fight against the Pennsylvania,
Philadelphia and Reading and other roads
for more than two days free storage time
on shipments received at Philadelphia
The Interstate Commerce Commission de-
cided that the roads rule limiting free
storage time to two days was justified
and not discriminatory.


However, In deciding this case the Com
mission gave one point of the victory to
the Commercial Exchange by requiring
the carriers to amend their storage rules
to provide for additional free storage time
when cars destined to any one consignee
are punched, through whatever cause. and
are delivered in accumulated numbers in
excess Of daily shipments


The fight against a limit of two days
free storage time began in November.
1914, Immediately after the carriers
amended their rules by changing the free
time from four to two days.


Tho Baltimore Chamber of Commerce
Joined the Philadelphia Exchange In its
fight against the rule. and In deciding the
cases today the commission made the
same ruling to apply at Baltimore as at
Philadelphia.


IN its decision the Interstate Commerce
Commission held that storage regulations
are lO prevent COHBtS-
ton of carriers terminal facilities, and
that public interests require that freight
should be removed promptly from the car
riers' terminals.


Many conslgnees took advantage Of the
four days free period previously allowed
at Philadelphia and unnecessarily allowed
their freight to remain in the freight sta
tions for the full period. Great conges-
tion resulted, which rendered 1t difficult
for "a conslgnee who desired 20 remove his
freight promptly to get II.


Defendants asserted that the two-day
period has eliminated such congestion and,
coupled with the increased capacity of the
freight houses. has improved conditions to
the satisfaction of shippers and teamsters
patronizing the freight stations. Formerly
from per cent. to 20 per cent of the
less-than-carload shipments received at
the various freight stations remained there
until the third day of the four-day free
period allowed. Substantially all such
freight Is now removed within the two
day period without any material increase
in the amount finally stored over that
stored when the four-day rule was in
effect.

London, July 1.-THE Russians
have won another great success in
Volhynia. The blows of General
Brussiloff's forces southwest of
Lutsk have swept the Austro- Ger
man armies behind the Lipa River.


"Under the protection Of a Ger
man counter attack" says to-night's
Austrian official statement, "the Teu-
tonic troops south of Lutsk were
withdrawn behind the Lower Lipa,
unmolested by the enemy"


At the same, time General Kuro-
patkin, the Russian commander in
the north, launched a violent offen-
sive against Won Hindenburg's lines
on the Dvina River, General Letchit-
sky extended his lines near Kirli-
baba. on the frontier Of Transyl-
vania, and the Cars forces in Vol
hynia bagged an additional $1,000
prisoners in one short day of fight
ing.


The latest great Russian advance
was won through intense artillery
preparation, followed by quick, pow
erful thrusts at points previously
tested and found to be insufficiently
strong to withstand any great press
ure.


Russians Pierce Foes Lines.


Hammering relentlessly at General
Won Linsingen's positions southeast OF
Sviniuchy and near Pustomyty and
Szklin, the Russians finally pierced the
Teuton lines along a mile front at the
latter point and penetrated several
miles into the territory so obstinately
held by the enemy for weeks.


This victory again illustrates the
power of the Russian thrusts, the abil-
ity Of the Cars commanders to strike
at any point along the whole Eastern
front-and to strike with consternating
suddenness-and the impotency o. the
German and Austrian armies, however
we'll reinforced, to stem the tide of the
Russian advance except along strongly
fortified natural barriers.


Russian Blow Sudden.


The Russians achieved the same re-
suit by the same methods when they
threw the German forces back from the
Styr to the Stokhod There the enor-
nous forces brought up by the Teutons
have temporarily checked the Russian
advance toward Kovel.


But while the entire attention Of the
Austrians and Germans was being CEN
tired on the Stokhod line, the Russians
were making their usual complete prep
arations for the drive south Ct Lutsk,
which to-day achieved its primary OBJ
iect. Then they struck quickly. For
the first time since the Germans halted
their progress on the Stokhod the Rus
slams took up the cudgels and welded
tnem WIN ihPANiNy
which swept the enemy off his feet and
sent him flying to cover.


Menace to Lemberg.


Military critics here are agreed that
the Russians have won a great tactical
success. The retirement of the Teu-
tons TO the Lipa and beyond greatly
increases the double menace to which
Kovel and Lemberg are exposed. Strik-
ing south across the Galician border.
only a few miles away, the Russians
would press the Teutons back over the
Bug River, and from that line threaten
Lemberg as it has not been threatened
before in the present drive.


Hitting north and northwest from
their newly won positions. they would
imperil the German lines along the
Stokhod to a flank attack, which prob
ably would result in the retirement of
the Teutons to the Vladimfr-Vo Volynski-
Kovel line. Their present lines on the
north bank of the Lips constitute the
gravest menace to those two important
places.

That the Russians are continuing their
attacks on the Galician front is indi-

issued yesterday in Petrograd, but by
official statements from both Berlin and
Vienna.


According to Berlin. strong Russian
forces made repeated attacks Saturday
on the Austro-German positions north
of Zboroff between the rivers Sereth
and StTipa. Russians penetrated the
German lines near Manaov. but were
driven out by counter attack. the
statement says. leaving more than 700
prisoners and seven machine guns in
the hands of the Teutons.


Battles Termed stubborn"


Both Petrograd and Vienna describe
the fighting as stubborn" Vienna ad-
mits slight Russian success in the
Carpathians. but says further attacks
were checked. Between Zboroff and the
upper Sereth. according to Vienna, Rus
slams captured Teutonic positions but
they were regained by a counter at
tack at night.

in two prisoners.

active than usual along the whole
front. The hostile batteries retalia ted
by bombarding our positions about

EMPOWERED in flowers and sur
rounded by houseful of friends, Nine.
Frances Aida gave her annual song
recital last night in Carnegie Hall.
Nine. Aida was in excellent voice--in
fact she has never been in better-and
received long, continued applause.


Perhaps her best singing was ac-
complshed In two unusually interest
ing Finnish songs, both of which were
being given here for the first time:
These were Merikanto's "Sinulle" and
Jaernefeld's "Kentolaulau," and the
soprano gave them with spirit and
nuance. Another charming song, we'll
sung. was Jacob Antonio Pertis
"Canzonetta," while Munro's Lovely
Celia" was also gracefully given, even
though the singers diction might here
have been clearer.


Nine. Alda's chief fault lay in lack
of variety Of expression and of tone
color, which caused slight monotony
of impression. It is evident, none the
less, that she has grown in interpretive
rover and that her tone production is
greatly improved. She sang last night
with ease. and she never felt called
upon to force her voice.


Among her other numbers were an
air from Johann Christian Bach's
"Carattaco," MozaS.'s mon so piri," n
song by Sibella, "Chanson d'Antonne,"
written for Nine Aida. and two songs
by Frank La Forge, likewise written
for her. Mr.. La Forge played her &C
compartments most gratefully.

When ] sit down to read at night

The painted cups, the mirror bright,
The crazy pattern on the wall.

Plucked from the bosom of the lea,

Remembering when it was a tree

To make this room rich, safe and warm,

They pass who built in blood this room,

you're too late. I've already called

Cosmetics are going up again.

rouges and powders so necessary accord

New Haven, June 3.-The Yale crews
left New Haven this afternoon for
Gales Ferry. Conn. where they will be-
gin the final period of training in nrep-
aration for the Yale Harvard race on
the Thames June % Twenty-one oars
men and two coxswains were included
in the varsity squad picked for the
final workouts.


The men left New Haven late this
afternoon aboard two steam yachts, the
Sultana, owned by Mrs. f. H. Harri-
man, and the Savarona, owned by
Colonel Robinson. of Hartford. Mrs.
Harriman's son, Roland, is a member Of
the Yale crew. while Colonel Robinson
has been interested in the Yale navy
for several seasons.


The oarsmen will spend tonight and
all day Sunday aboard the yachts.
There will be no hurry, and the boats
will proceed et low rate Of speed 10
allow the oarsmen all possible benefit
from the fresh air and sunshine on the
Sound II is planned 20 reach Gales
Ferry. located seven miles up the river
from New London, Sunday evening.


The last weeks work has been a
strenuous one, and the men are in need
of race The Yale crew situation has
been topsy-turvy since the Blue was
defeated a week ago by Cornell and
Princeton, and Guy Nickalls has chosen
the hard work method of leading the
oarsmen out of the wilderness. Last
Monday he made an absolutely fresh
start Two crews were picked. of as
nearly equal ability as possible, and
there have been daily races between
them. Frequent changes have been
made in these boats, and pair-oared
work has been feature Of each days
drill.


Nickalls's failure to pick first and
second varsity crews for the final prac-
tice yesterday came somewhat as sur
rise. The coach has apparently left
his decision until he gets his men well
settled in their new quarters. There
will be crew work at Gales Ferry on
Monday. and the first selection of the
regular boats will probably not De made
until Wednesday. That was the way
Nckalls felt about the matter when he
left New Haven tonight.


DESPITE this weeks disheartening
showing and defeats at the hands OF
Pennsylvania, Princeton and Cornell in
turn, Yale oarsmen and close followers
of the sport are not downhearted about
the outlook. The defeats have accom-
plished one very important thing. The
crew men no longer place blind trust
in the belief that Nickalls will pull
them through. They have come to re-
alize that what they accomplish must
be done BY their own efforts. Further
more, fighting spirit, such as has not
been evident all season, has been
aroused. and every man will be on his
mettle at Gales Ferry.

Manufacturers Advantages


1t is well known within the automobile in
dustry that large manufacturers, with $1O,-
100000 to $4,000, 900 invested in complete

Manufacturers producing $4,000 cars an
nually produce more parts of a specific type
than any parts manufacturer produces. AS
rule, parts manufacturers are not specialists in
the sense that they make only one type of body
or axle or engine. Although their total output
may sometimes (but rarely) exceed the guam
tity of any large automobile manufacturer,
they make numerous varieties, and hence do
not obtain as low manufacturing costs as the
large automobile manufacturer obtains


Hence, the large automobile manufacturer
produces his own parts at lower cost than the
parts manufacturer produces similar parts for
an assembler who buys in small quantities, and
it follows that the 23% excess cost of the assem-
bier illustrated above is not exaggerated.


Another point is that the assembler, buying
parts from numerous sources, and often the
same part from several sources, cannot obtain
the same precision of machining and assem-
bling in the finished car which the large manu-
facturer obtains.

larger than the manufacturers profit, because
the assembler usually sells only few thousand
cars annually. The illustration shows that this
profit is 60% more than the manufacturer re-

overstated Also the dealers discount is

text:
Football affairs at Columbia are
reaching a crisis.


swarthmore, Wesleyan and New YORK
University are to be met on the GRID
iron. and the Blue and White squad Is
shot to pieces by injuries. Nelson Met
calf has had no easy time OF 1t this
year. and, just at the time when his
team began TO find itself and work as
a machine, JEFF Healy was cut down.
This is the most serious loss OF all, for
Healy was frst-class player, who' IN
the opinion of keen judges, would win
his place on almost any college team
in the country.


The loss of Healy comes as the cui-
minating misfortune Of a streak that
has logged the Columbia team
throughout the season. When Howard
Miller injured his knee early in the
season the green-eyed jinx rubbed his
hands and smiled, and then set about
the work of reducing the squad.


One after one the players were hurt
and kept out of action. Sterling Van
de Water, guard; Bud WILDER, tackle;
Joe Hegeman, a back; Raimando, quar-
terback; Jimmy Rosen, back; Vollmer,
line man; Munroe. back; Raegner, line
man; Cochran, line man and back, and
Jimmy Cleveland, line man, are among
the more prominent men who are nurs-
ing injuries of various natures.


Injuries Numerous


Munroe has a sprained wrist, Raj
mando a broken collarbone, and Cleve.
lands ribs are damaged, but mostly all
the other fellows are suffering from IN
juries to their legs.


To be sure, the greater number OF
these boys will be ready to take their
places in the games to come, but the
fact remains that they are not at their
best and hard wallop may drive them
to the side lines.


The Swarthmore game will be moth
ing of the tango tea variety. The
Pennsylvania team has cleaned up for
Lafayette, Pennsylvania, Franklin and
Marshall and Ursinus and Johns Hop
kins, while only fifteen points have
been scored against them. Swarthmore
has not a smashing, man-killing team,
but it is powerful and we'll balanced
and thus far has always been able to
develop sufficient power to win.


These days are devoted to expert
menting with the Columbia line. Hand
icapped by injuries to his best men,
Metcalf has been forced to develop
versatility among those who are physi-
cally fit, and throughout the long sig
nal and formation drill he worked his
line men in various positions. Jimmy
Cleveland was moved to right tackle
and then to his place at guard, while
Raegner played tackle and guard also.
Bud WILDER and Sterling Van de Water
moved around in the first line.


Lack of Aggressiveness


For all the beef and Drawn in the
Columbia line there is a noticeable
lack Of aggressiveness, or. to be more
exact, perhaps, wisely directed agrees
siveness. This was brought to light in
the Stevens game. The men are prone
to look for the play first, then charge
and finally, if possible, block. Against
well coached, aggressive team, how
ever, the delay necessitated by stop
ping to look first will prove fatal. 1t
will give the opposing first line the
opportunity to get the first lunge and
then carry through to clean up the
secondaries. An old established rule in
football demands that the line charge
first, then find the play, if possible. and
finally block. The secondaries will find
the play, meet it and tackle or block
as the necessity arises.


Long Signal Drill


The signal drill lasted until long
after shutdown yesterday, and the white
ball was finally called into play. The
varsity lineup was as follows: Ken
nedy, left end; WILDER, left tackle;
Donaldson, left guard; Brown, centre;
Raegner, right guard; Cleveland, right
tackle; Cochran, right end; McCabe,
quarterback; Dunn, left halfback; |. T.
Rosen, fullback; Hegeman, right half
back.


Swarthmore will probably take the
field against Columbia as follows:
Smith, left end; McGovern, left tackle:
Wilson, left guard; Ridpath, centre;
Stow. right guard; Endicott, right
tackle; DIN, right end; Johnson, quar-
terback; Baker, right halfback; Mi
chael, left halfback, and Bush, full
back.


Smith, Ridpath, Endicott and Bush
are men Of reputation, and are expected
to play a WhirlWind game.

Early in the evening a squadron OF

loaded down with explosives, set out

great height.


Less than three hours later the huge

followed was among the most dramatic
of the war. Nine Allied and six Ger

came to an end.

LONDON Aug. 2S.-The Germans made
two determined attempts last night to
wrest from the British newly captured
positions south of Thiepval, which menace
that German stronghold.


General Haig reported this afternoon that
both attacks were repulsed. though in one
attempt the Germans gained temporary
footing in the British trenches. The Ger
man losses we're described as heavy.


The British troops have succeeded in
holding the ground recently won, despite
the desperate efforts OF the Germans to dis
lodge them.


BERLIN, Aug. 23--British forces that
are trying to encircle the German position
at Thiepval. on the Sonime front, renewed
their assaults last night, but all were re-
pulsed.


This information was contained in the
official statement issued by the War Office
today.


The British attacked along the Pozieres.
Thiepval road, but were unable to push
their lines forward because of the hot fire
from German artillery and machine guns.

NEW YORK May 22-An army of 10000
women, moblized from the ranks of 2,000,-
900 clubwomen in every State and posses
sion of the United States, began the inva-
sion of Manhattan Isle today for the open
ing of the 18th biennial convention of the
Federated Women's Clubs of America In
the Seventh Regiment armory here tomor-
row.


AS the squads. companies regiments and
battalions of handsomely gowned femininity
troop along the platforms from the long
trains pulling into Grand Central, Pennsyl.
vania Station and Hudson Terminal, from
California, Florida, Maine and other parts
of the country, they are taken in hand by
Boy Scouts in khaki, who see them safely
delivered" to their appointed places Other
scouts go around afterward and give them
printed and oral instructions about getting
here and there in New York. Still other
scouts look after their luggage.


Thanks to these lads and the hard work
ing arrangements committee, under the d.
rection of Mrs. North Mclean, of the New
York Federation, the 10000 will be COM
fortably settled in New York town and on
their way to hear Mrs. Percy V. Penny
hacker, of Texas, bang the big gavel on the
steel sounding board that will call the con-
vention to order.


Today's program for the delegates was
largely social. There was big luncheon
and there will be equally big dinner,
with the purely routine task OF registering
and organizing the convention on the side.
Presidential politics-referrng to the presi-
dency of the federated clubs and not the
Presidency of the United States-was al
ready bubbling over today. 1t will be the
East against the West in this struggle
Mrs. Samuel b. Sheath, of Tiffin, O., against
Mrs. Josiah Evans Cowles, of Los Angeles
Some fervid forensic forums are predicted


From the moment the convention Is
called to order until the night of June 2,
the women leaders of the nation will
make this old town hum with speeches
and squabbles and social affairs and all
those other exciting events that women
bring about when they get together. They
will give the world their official opinion on
government and goulash, food and fight
ing, marriage and millionaires, babies and
bantng, health and hardressing, short
skirts and short ballots, big wives and
little husbands, prizefghts and teahghts,
and many, many other matters of general
interest.


There has been evidence of some rather
sharp feeling between the city and country
delegates over the matter of style which
may crop up in some form during the con-
vention


The only open display of feeling on the
point thus far comes from the Indiana dele
CATION whose members have expressed
themselves being quietly determined to
ignore advice and instructions from New
York, distributed gratis through the Fed
eration's magazines telling how to dress
while here.

Washington, April 2l.-Serious prob

situation brought about by the Euro

partment say the service already has
suffered heavily and may be seriously
impaired II the war continues much
longer.

of living has risen enormously nearly
all over the world and has reduced
many consuls 20 the verge of starva-
ton. designations have been threat
ened in many cases, but some consuls

military camp at Brownsville. The
camps of the New York National Guards

aced sections has been paralyzed, and
only few details of the great storm

United States army radio station at Fort
Sam Houston.

the heaviest damage Tents are torn
down and torrential rains have turned
the country into a morass. Regulars and
Illinois, Iowa, and Virginia regiments to-
night are quartered in Brownsville. in
the city hall. courthouse, and public
buildings. They have two days rations
with them.


Maj. Gen. Funston has been unable to
get any word whatever from the New
York militia camps at McAuen. Pharr
and Mission. The majority of the New
York troops were away from their base
on long hike, and the only protection
they had from the storm was pup
tents


The last message received at Calves
ton from Brownsville at 3 o'clock this
afternoon said: High winds and heavy
rains Growing worse" Previous To
this, Point Isabel reported: Winds Of
hurricane force"

MOBILE, Ala, October 19.-Southern

100000.

power wires. when the wind attained
it's maximum velocity several persons
were blown through plate-glass win
dows, but they escaped serious injury.

woman-was caused by the falling OF
live wire into the street.

well as other buildings unroofed. The
electric light plant also was put out OF
commission and all wires were down for
twelve hours, the city being cut off from
communication with the outside world for
that length of time. Train service from
Pensacola to Jacksonville will be sus-
pended for a week as the result of dam
age to the tracks.


Marine damage was great, both in this
harbor and at the Florida port. Two
small vessels here sank, while four others
were driven ashore. In addition. num-

was shot and killed year and half

by cattle rustlers near the Scott ranch,
fourteen miles northwest of Trinidad.

murdered boy, met his death while

Fucurino was found guilty of the muir

do not believe the two murders have

According to the Paris Petit Journal the
Germans are compelling the civil population
10 evacuate the three French cities of Lille
R5ubaix and Tourcoing, which lie just be-
hind the German lines in the west along
the front where, as last nights official bull
lerin announces, the British artillery and
infantry are manifesting steadily increas-
Ing activity.


.The Petit Journal says Premier BRAND
is preparing a formal protest to all neutral
nations against this action OF the German
military authorities on the ground that 1t
Is contrary to The Hague conventions.


Last nights official bulletin indicates
that the raids into the German lines. which
have been going on incessantly for the last
four days, have not only been increasing
in number, but have been carried out on a
steadily wider scale and with more and
more considerable results in the way Of
German prisoners.


At the same time the British artillery
has never for one moment let up in its
steady, relentless pounding of the German
lines, Dispatches from headquarters say
the results OF the tremendous artillery fire
are becoming more and more evident in the
destruction of the German fortifcatlons.


The text of the official statement of the
British War ONCE followD:


During the last "a hours a large


number Of our accommodating and raid


ing parties entered the enemy's trenches


at various points along the entire front
of the British army.


All these enterprises were success


ful in achieving their object. infiicting


heavy casualties on the Germans and


capturing prisoners and war stores


In several instances our troops re-


manned for considerable period in the


German lines repulsing counter-attacks


across the open.


One OF these enterprises took place


after the discharge of gas. our troops,


entering the German trenches. found


q considerable number OF dead. Our


casualties were Insignificant.


The artillery OF both sides has been


active along the front, Hostile trenches


were much damaged in many places.


The intermittent discharge of smoke


and gas has aroused the activities OF


the enemy's guns and caused him to


disclose his battery positions.


A dispatch last night from British head
quarters says this German return fire has
been generally ineffective, although in places
the German guns have been very active,
They have used large number OF lachry-
matory (tear-producing) shells.


The incessant British raids this dispatch
says. striking the German lines now here,
now there. has had the effect OF keeping the
Germans on the alert everywhere, and
there are indications that they are becoming
nervous under the constant strain. The
Australian troops, the Highland Light In
fantry. ths lancaster Fusiliers and the
Ltverpools are mentioned as regiments
